1. Introduction
Received22NOV2019
Accepted10APR2020
PangeaisthemostrecentsupercontinenttohaveevolvedinEarth'slonghistory,formingat~320Mafrom
Acceptedarticleonline16APR2020
the mergerof two other large landmasses,Laurussia andGondwana(Rogers, 1996; Stampfliet al.,2013;
Unrug, 1996; Wegener, 1912). Although the reconstruction of the major blocks of Pangea is now mostly
established(Domeieretal.,2012;Torsviketal.,2012),thelatePaleozoicpositionsofmanyofthecontinental
blocksofEastAsia,whichwerelargelyindependentofPangeathen,remainuncertain(e.g.,Collins,2003;
Golonkaetal.,2006;Huangetal.,2018;Metcalfe,2009;Unrug,1996).Themainreasonforthisisthatmany
ofthecontinentalblocksofEastAsiaarecomposedofsmallterranesormicrocontinentalblocks,themove-
mentsofwhichmayhavebeencomplexduringthelatePaleozoic.Althoughstratigraphiccorrelationand
thequalitativecomparisonoffossilsfromdifferentblockshavebeeninvaluabletoolsinthecraftingofrecon-
structions for East Asia, they generally yield nonunique solutions (e.g., Berthelin et al., 2003;
Metcalfe, 2006, 2013). Paleomagnetism, as the only quantitative reconstruction tool available for
pre‐Mesozoic time, has been invaluable in determining the ancient latitudes and azimuthal orientations
of continents, but it cannot directly estimate paleolongitude. Although paleolongitudes can theoretically
be constrained from paleomagnetic Euler pole analysis (Gordon et al., 1984; Wu et al., 2017; Wu &
Kravchinsky,2014),suchanalysesstrictlyrequire“complete”high‐resolutionapparentpolarwanderpaths
thatarenotavailableformanysmallAsianblocks.
ThetectonicblockofTarimisoneoftheprincipalcratoniccomponentsofEastAsia,butthereisdisagree-
menton howTarimwaspositioned inthe Paleo‐Asian andTethystectonic systemsof the latePaleozoic
(Usui&Tian,2017;Xuetal.,2011;Xuetal.,2014;Yangetal.,2007),anddifferentscholarshaverestored
Tarim differently with respect to Pangea. For example, in the reconstruction of Golonka et al. (2006),
©2020.AmericanGeophysicalUnion.
AllRightsReserved. Tarim is in contact with the north China block in the early Permian (their 296–285 Ma map), whereas

### page_2
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2019JB019111
Scotese(2004)depictawideoceanbetweenTarimandthenorthChinablockat306Ma.Somehavepre-
ferredtopositionTarimalongsideKazakhstanintheearlyPermian(Metcalfe,2009;Şengöretal.,2014),
and yet others have omitted Tarim altogether owing to its paleogeographic uncertainties (e.g., Torsvik
etal.,2012).PartofthisuncertaintyinthelatePaleozoicpaleogeographicpositioningofTarimstemsfrom
poorlydescribedlegacypaleomagneticdatathatweremostlycollectedinthe1980s.Therefore,wepresent
theresultsofanewpaleomagneticstudyofearlyPermianrocksfromTarimthatmeetstricterreliability
criteria.
FollowingWilson's(1963)recognitionofhotspots,Morgan(1971)proposedthathotspotsarethesurface
manifestationofmantleplumesemanatingfromthedeepmantleandsuggestedthattheyplayanimportant
roleinglobalgeodynamics.Shortlyafterward,itwasrecognizedthathotspots(andthustheplumesthat
feed them) seemed to spatially correlate with seismically imaged structures in the deepest mantle
(Chase,1979;Crough&Jurdy,1980),nowcalledlargelowshearvelocityprovinces(LLSVPs).Morerecently,
ithasbeenshownthatthisspatialcorrelationbetweenplumesandtheLLSVPs(astheyarepositionedat
present) can be extended backward to at least 300 Ma by using reconstructed large igneous provinces
(LIPs)andkimberlitesasaproxyformantleplumes(Burke&Torsvik,2004;Kuzminetal.,2010;Torsvik
et al., 2008, 2010). On the basis of this observed correlation between reconstructed LIPs and LLSVPs,
Burkeetal.(2008)definedtheconceptofplumegenerationzones(PGZs)asregionsofthelowermostmantle
(alongthemarginsoftheLLSVPs)wheremantleplumesoriginateandspecificallypostulatedthatthePGZs
maybespatiallystablebackwardintime.Torsviketal.(2014)subsequentlyformalizedthisPGZconceptasa
meansbywhichtobuildabsolutereconstructions(involvingtherestorationofbothlatitudeandlongitude)
throughoutthePhanerozoic.Accordingtothismethodology,theancientlatitudeofagivencontinentcanbe
determinedfrompaleomagneticdata,and—ifthatsamecontinenthostsaLIPorkimberlitesthatformed
during the time of interest—its paleolongitude can be constrained to a location above one of the
LLSVPmargins.
BecausetheearlyPermianintraplatemagmaticrocksofTarimarethoughttoconstituteaLIP(Xuetal.,2014;
Zhangetal.,2010),weaimtousenewpaleomagneticdatafromtheserocksinconjunctionwiththePGZ
reconstructionmethodtodeterminetheabsolutepositionofTarimintheearlyPermian.
2. Geological Setting andPaleomagnetic Sampling
TarimisoneofthreemaincratonicblocksthattogethercomprisemainlandChina(theothertwobeingthe
northandsouthChinablocks).TarimissurroundedbytheTianshanorogenicbelt(tothenorth),theKunlun
orogenicbelt(tothesouth),andtheAltynorogenicbelt(tothesoutheast)(Figure1).IntheearlyPermian,
Tarimwascharacterizedbyvoluminousmagmatism,resultinginmagmaticrockadditionsthatareestimated
tocompriseatotalareaofmorethan250,000km2andavolumeofmorethan300,000km3(Tianetal.,2010;
Yangetal.,2007),thuspossiblyformingoneofthelargestLIPsinAsia.Inrecentyears,importantprogress
hasbeenmadeincharacterizingandrefiningthegeochronologyandgeochemistryoftheTarimLIP(here-
after “TLIP”) (Chen et al., 2006; Li et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2010; Usui &
Tian, 2017; Wei et al., 2014, 2015; Yang et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2011, 2017; Zou et al., 2013, 2015).
GeochronologicaldataindicatethatthedurationofmagmatismassociatedwiththeTLIPcouldhavespanned
~20 Myr, but the flood basalts that erupted at 291–287 Ma probably constitute its main phase (Chen
etal.,2010;Xuetal.,2014).GeochemicaldataindicatethatthesePermianbasaltsareoftypicaloceanicisland
basaltaffinity(Yuetal.,2009;Yuetal.,2011;Zhouetal.,2009).Theassociationoftheserockstoamantle
plumeisfurthersuggestedbytheoccurrenceofhigh‐Mgpicrites(Tianetal.,2010;Yuetal.,2009).
Geographically,thevolcanicrocksoftheTLIParemostlylocatedinthewesternpartoftheTarimBasin.
Theyarewidelyexposedinsurfaceoutcropsandarealsointersectedindrillcoresandrecognizedinseismic
exploration surveys (Tian et al., 2010). Lithologically, they are mainly composed of basic volcanic rocks,
includingbasalt,diabase,basalticandesiteandultrabasicrocks.Basicrocksareexposedinthesectionsof
Yingan,Sishichang,Kaipaizileike,Damusi,Qipan,Xiahenan,andGudongshan(Figure1b),whereasmore
acidicrocksandultrabasicrocksarefoundintheareasofXiaohaiziandWajilitage(Figure1b)(Yu,2009).
ThepaleomagneticsamplesinthisstudyweremainlycollectedfromtheKepingareainthenorthwestern
part of the Tarim block. The strata exposed in this area are Sinian (mid‐to late Neoproterozoic) to
Permian and Neogene in age (Figure 2). The basalts are mainly located in Lower Permian strata, which

Figure1.(a)TectonicpositionoftheTarimblockinAsiaand(b)geotectonicunitsofTarimBasinandthedistributionoftheTLIP(modifiedafterZouetal.,2015;
Yangetal.,2013).Abbreviations:Dms(Damusi);Gds(Gudongshan);Kpz(Kaipaizileike);Qp(Qipan);Ssc(Sishichang);Wjl(Wajilitage);Xhn(Xiahenan);Xhz
(Xiaohaizi);Yg(Yingan).
comprisethe Kupukuziman Formation andthe overlying KaipaizileikeFormation. These formations are
exposed along ESE‐ and ENE‐trending homoclines that are divided by a major fault (the Ingan Fault)
(Figure 2). The Kupukuziman Formation conformably covers Upper Carboniferous rocks of the
KangkelinFormation,andtheKaipaizileikeFormationisunconformablycoveredbyNeogenerocks.The
KupukuzimanandKaipaizileikeFormationswerefoldedbeforethedepositionoftheNeogenerocks,and
inthe context of the regionalgeology, itis assumedthat foldingprincipally occurred inassociationwith
tectonismrelatedtoIndia‐Asiacollision(Allenetal.,1999;Ni,1978;Yinetal.,1998;Zhangetal.,2016).
However,youngerdeformationisalsoobservedinthearea;forexample,theInganFaultwasactiveinthe
PliocenetoEarlyPleistocene(Zhangetal.,2013).
Thebasaltsoftheseformationsoccurinflowsequences,eachrepresentingmultipleeruptions.Atthebaseof
eachsequenceisoneormorewell‐consolidatedflows,usuallywithcolumnarjointingorblockybasalt,and
atthetopisvolcanicbrecciaortuff(Chenetal.,2006;Yuetal.,2010).TheKupukuzimanFormationhastwo
basaltsequences(I1andI2);thethicknessofthefirstsequence(I1)isapproximately45m,andthesecond
sequence(I2)isapproximately85m.TheKaipaizileikeFormationhassixsequences(II1–II6),withacumu-
lativemaximumthicknessof450m(Figure3).
Paleomagnetic samples were collected from three sections: Sichishang (Ssc; 40.828°N, 79.848°E),
Kaipaizileike (Kpz; 40.744°N, 79.743°E), and Yingan (Yg; 40.641°N, 79.560°E) (Figure 2). Isotopic ages

determined from the Kupukuziman and Kaipaizileike Formations at these three sampling sections
(Table 1) demonstrate the age of the basalts to range from 295 to 281 Ma, with an average age of
287.6 ± 2.7 Ma. A total of 490 samples were collected from 60 sites: 33 sites at Ssc, 21 sites at Kpz, and
6 sites at Yg. Sites in volcanic rocks are defined by multiple samples from an individual flow, whereas
sedimentary sites can include samples from several sedimentary layers and therefore may record some
secular variation at the site level.
Ofthe33sitesfromtheSscsectionoftheKupukuzimanFormation(Figure4a),19werecollectedfromtheI1
basaltsandtheirunderlyingstrata(SitesA03–A21;131samples),whichincludedsamplesofbasalt,sand-
stoneandlimestone.FourteensiteswerecollectedfromtheI2basalts(SitesD01–14;190samples).
Ofthe21sitesfromtheKpzsection,onesitewascollectedfromthesandstonelayerbetweenII2andII3(site
C01;sixsamples),andfoursites(sitesC02–C05;27samples)werecollectedfromtheII3basalts.Eightsites
(sitesC06–C13;54samples)werecollectedfromtheII4basalts,andeightsites(sitesC14–C21;51samples)
werecollectedfromtheII5basalts.

AttheYgsectionoftheKaipaizileikeFormation,sixsites(SitesB01–B06;31samples)werecollectedfrom
theII2basaltsandtheirunderlyingstrata.ThissectionofthePermianstratahasadifferentstructuralatti-
tudethantheothertwosectionsandthereforepresentstheopportunityforafoldtest.Notably,theasso-
ciated geologic structures do not represent a simple fold about a horizontal fold axis and may rather
belongtodifferentfold/faultsystems(Zhangetal.,2013);the“foldtest”inthiscaseismoreaccuratelya
regionaltilttest(hereafter“foldtest”sensulato).
Sampleswerecollectedusingagasoline‐powereddrillandwereorientedinsituusingmagneticandsolar
compasses.AhandheldGPSunitwasusedtodeterminethegeographiccoordinatesofthesamplingsites
andbeddingorientationsofthesedimentaryrocksweremeasuredwithamagneticcompass.
3. Results
Rockmagneticexperimentsdesignedtocharacterizethemineralogicalcarriersofmagneticremanencewere
performed in the Paleomagnetic Laboratory of Northwest University (Xi'an) and the laboratory of
Geomagnetism and Chronology at the Institute of Geology and Geophysics (Chinese Academy of
Sciences,Beijing).Isothermalremanentmagnetization(IRM)experimentsandmagneticsusceptibilityver-
sustemperature(k‐T)experimentswereperformedon27samplesselectedfromboththeKupukuzimanand
KaipaizileikeFormations.IRMexperimentswereperformedwithanASCIM‐10‐30pulsemagnetizeranda
JR‐6Amagnetometer,andk‐TexperimentswereconductedinanargonatmosphereusinganMFK2suscept-
ibilitymeteranditsCS‐4temperaturecontrolsystem.
Thermaldemagnetizationwasusedtostudythestabilityofsampleremanenceanditsconstituentcompo-
nentswiththeuseofanMMTD‐48oven.Thermaldemagnetizationfollowedprogressivestepsof50–100°
C(below450°C)and10–25°C(above450°C),andfollowingeachstep,thesamplesweremeasuredwith
a2G‐755Rsuperconducting(cryogenic)magnetometerorJR‐6Aspinnermagnetometer.Theseexperiments
were carried out in the laboratory of Geomagnetism and Chronology at the Institute of Geology and
Geophysics,ChineseAcademyofSciences;theLaboratoryofStructuralMagnetismatPekingUniversity;
andthePaleomagneticLaboratoryatNorthwestUniversity.Vectoranalysisofthemeasuredmagneticdirec-
tionswasperformedusingorthogonalvectordiagrams(Zijderveld,1964)andprincipalcomponentanalysis
(PCA)toidentifyandquantifydiscretemagneticcomponents(Kirschvink,1980).Sitemeanpaleomagnetic
directionswerecalculatedusingthestandardFisherstatistics(Fisher,1953)viaPMGSC(Enkin,1990)and
PaleoMac6.5(Cogné,2003)software.
3.1. RockMagneticResults
TheresultsofrepresentativerockmagneticexperimentsareshowninFigure5.
TheIRMcurvesofsandstonesamples(Figure5a)climbrapidlyinappliedfieldsbelow200mTbutdonot
reachcompletesaturationevenat2.5T.Adeclineinthemagneticsusceptibilityofthesandstoneisobserved
above~550°Candcontinuesto~650°C(Figures5band5c),whichsuggeststhepresenceofbothmagnetite
andhematite.
TheIRMvaluesofthelimestonesamplesalsoclimbupto1.5Tbutdonotreachcompletesaturationevenat
2.5T.Thisindicatesthatthelimestonescontainbothlow‐coercivityandhigh‐coercivitymagneticminerals
(Figure5d).Thek‐TcurvesshowadistinctHopkinsonpeak,followedbyaninflectionatapproximately580°
C,afterwhichthesusceptibilitydropstoverylowvalues(Figures5eand5f).
TheIRMcurvesofthetuffsamplessaturatequicklyunderalowexternalfieldof~200mT(Figure5g),indi-
catingthatthemagneticmineralsinthetuffsamplesaremostlyoflowcoercivity.Thek‐Tcurvesshowthat
the magnetic susceptibility of the tuffs drops slightly between temperatures of 300 to 400 °C andrapidly
dropstoverylowvalueswhenheatedto580°C(Figures5hand5i).Weinterpretsuchbehaviortoindicate
thepresenceofmagnetiteandtitanium‐richmagnetite.
TherockmagneticbehaviorsofthebasaltsamplesareshowninFigures5j–5l.TheIRMresultsshowthatthe
basaltsreachsaturationwhentheappliedfieldissmall(0–300mT),indicatingthatthemagneticmineralogy
isdeterminedbythepresenceofalow‐coercivitymineral.Thek‐Tcurvesshowthatthemagneticsuscept-
ibilityofthesampledecreasesrapidlyatapproximately450°Candreacheszeroatapproximately585°C.

3.2. PaleomagneticResults
Samples from each type of rock—sandstone, limestone, tuff, and basalt—were subjected to thermal
demagnetization. Demagnetization of the sandstone samples revealed two‐component behavior
(Figures 6a and 6b). A low‐temperature remanent component (LTC) was removed by approximately
250 °C, after which a high‐temperature characteristic remanent component (ChRM) trended directly to
the origin. Most sandstone samples maintained a stable remanence up to 690 °C (Figure 6b), although
some were demagnetized by 585 °C (Figure 6a), suggesting that both magnetite and hematite (the pre-
sence of which is demonstrated by the magnetic mineralogy experiments described above) are carriers
of the magnetic remanence. The ChRM of these samples was therefore defined within the temperature
rangeof250–690or250–585°C;thevectorsfittedtothesetwotemperaturerangesaredirectionallyindis-
tinguishable (Figures 6a and 6b).
Thelimestonesamplestypicallyexhibitedtwo‐componentbehavior(Figures6cand6d).However,thenat-
uralremanenceofmostlimestonesampleswaslow(approximately1e−5A/m)anddecreasedrapidlywith
theonsetofthermaldemagnetization,sowewereabletodefineaChRMtrendingtotheoriginfromonlya
fewlimestonesites.Intheseexamples(Figures6cand6d),theLTCwasusuallyremovedbelow150°C,and
theChRMwasdefinedbetween200–565°C.Thermaldemagnetizationresultscombinedwiththerockmag-
netic results suggest that the remanence in the limestone samples is carried by magnetite and
possiblygoethite.
Demagnetizationofthetuffsamplesalsoexhibitedtwo‐componentbehavior(Figures6eand6f);aLTCwas
removedbyapproximately250°C,followedbyalineardecaytowardtheoriginby585°C.Ourdefinitionof
theChRMfromthetuffsampleswasthustypicallytakenwithinthetemperaturerangeof300–585°C.These

4. Discussion
4.1. AgeoftheMagnetization
ThepositiveresultofthefoldtestindicatesthattheChRMwasacquired
prior to folding. However, the age of folding of the basalts is poorly
known; it could have been due to Mesozoic tectonism associated with
Tarim's amalgamation with Central Asia and/or a result of the
India‐AsiacollisioninthePaleogene,buttheearliestdirectageconstraint
isprovidedbytheNeogeneageofthesedimentaryrockslyingunconform-
ablyabovethesampledsections.Nevertheless,thefoldtestresultssuggest
thattheChRMcouldbeaprimarymagnetization,andthereareseveral
additional observations that support such an interpretation.The first of
theseistheobservationthatthesameChRMhasbeenidentifiedinboth
the volcanic and sedimentary rocks (Figure 8a) andis evidently carried
bymagnetite,titanium‐richmagnetite,andhematite.Theobservationof

4.2. ComparisonWithPublishedPoles
TheFisherianmeanofoursitemeandirectionsconvertedtovirtualgeomagneticpoles(VGPs)yieldsanew
earlyPermianpaleomagneticpole:50.1°N,170.5°E,A =3.6°.Thispole(hereafterpole“T”)fallscloseto
95
severalotherpaleomagneticpolesforTarimintheearlyPermian(Figure9).Unfortunately,theearlierstu-
dieseitherlackedfieldstabilitytests(Baietal.,1987;Chengetal.,1983)orwerebasedonfewersamples,
sites, and sections (Fang et al., 1991; Li et al., 1988; Sharps et al., 1989), and few of them used the PCA
method,andthus,weconsiderournewresultthemostreliable.
ItisworthnotingthatmanyofthesepreexistingearlyPermianpaleomagneticpolesfromTarimfitalonga
small‐circlepassingthroughournewpoleandcenteredonthesamplingsite(Figure9),suggestingthatsmall
vertical‐axisrotationsmayhavevariouslyperturbedthedirectionaldatafromthisregion.However,compar-
isonofournewpoleagainsttheearlyPermianreferencepolesfromthesurroundingcratons(Table3and
Figure9)showsthatpoleTisclosetothe290MameanpolesfromSiberiaandtheEastEuropeanCraton
(Baltica),aswellasanearlyPermianpole(~286Ma)fromeasternKazakhstan,withwhichTarimamalga-
matedinthelatePermianandTriassic(Levashovaetal.,2003;Zhangetal.,2016).Thedirectionalsimilarity
ofpoleTwiththesecratonicreferencepoleswouldseemtosuggestthatifanyvertical‐axisrotationshave
affectedpoleT,theywereminor.WealsonotealargedifferencebetweenpoleTandcoevalreferencepoles
fromnorthChinaandsouthChina(bothinterpolatedbyHuangetal.,2018),indicatingthatTarim,north
ChinaandsouthChinahadnotfullyamalgamatedbythistime.

4.3. PaleogeographyofTarimandTLIPintheEarlyPermian
Lietal.(2014)estimatedthatthecenteroftheTLIPwaslocatedinthenortheasternpartoftheKepingarea,
andwethereforeconsideredthecoordinates41°N,80°EastheapproximatecenteroftheTLIP.Usingour
new paleomagnetic pole, we calculated that this center was located at a paleolatitude of 29.9°N ± 3.6 at
~288Ma,whichiseffectivelyidenticaltothepaleolatitudedeterminedfromasmall‐circlefittoalltheearly
PermianpaleomagneticpolesfromTarim,whichyieldedavalueof30.1°N±4.6.
WiththeearlyPermianpaleolatitudeoftheTLIPestablished,wecanevaluateitspaleolongitude.Plantfos-
sils,spores,andpollensuggestthattherewasprobablynotalargelongitudinalseparationofTarim,Siberia,
Europe,andKazakhstanduringtheearlyPermian(Dengetal.,2009;Zhu,2001),andthegeologicalrecord
demonstrates that these blocks were beginning to amalgamate with one another during Permian time
(Domeier&Torsvik,2014).WethereforetentativelypositionTarimslightlyeastofKazakhstanatthistime,
butwefurtherconsiderthealternativepossibilityofrestoringthelongitudeoftheTLIPusingthePGZrecon-
structionmethod(Torsviketal.,2014).
AccordingtotheassumptionsofthePGZmethod,mostLIPsareproducedbyplumesthatrisefromtheedges
oftheLLSVPsinthelowermostmantle(Burkeetal.,2008).TheLLSVPsoccurastwolarge,near‐equatorial
andapproximatelyantipodalbodieslocatedbeneathAfricaandthePacific,butasmaller,possiblyindepen-
dentanomalycalled“Perm”alsooccurstothenortheastofthemainAfricanLLSVP(Lekicetal.,2012).The
edgesoftheLLSVPshavebeenvariouslydefinedbutaregenerallytakenasthelocallysharpestlateralseismic
velocitygradientinthelowermostmantle,andhereweadopttheedgesasdefinedbyDoubrovineetal.(2016)

usingtheirs10meanaveragetomographymodel(Figure10).FollowingtheapproachofTorsviketal.(2014),
weseektorestoreTLIPtotheedgeofoneoftheLLSVPsafterapplyingacorrectionfortruepolarwander
(TPW).TPWisarotationoftheentiresolidEarth(crustandmantletogether)thatoccursduetochanges
initsinternalmassdistribution,whichaffecttheplanetarymomentofinertia(Gold,1955).Paleomagnetic
data, in measuring the displacement of continents relative to the spin axis, record a composite of both
individual plate motion and TPW. Thus, to be able to directly compare paleomagnetic‐based plate
reconstructions with (present‐day) mantle structures, TPW needs to be either subtracted from the plate
reconstruction or applied to the present‐day mantle structure. Accordingly, we apply the 290 Ma TPW
estimateofTorsviketal.(2014)—a7°rotationaboutapoleat0°N,11°E—totheLLSVPsinFigure10.
Givenourpaleolatitudeconstraints,thereareonlytwopossiblelocationswhereTarimcanberepositioned
directlyabovethemarginofoneoftheLLSVPs(Figure10),butthesewereoccupiedbytheEastEuropean
CratonandLaurentiaaccordingtothemodelofTorsviketal.(2014).However,ifwerelaxtherequirementto
fitTLIPdirectlyaboveanLLSVPmargin,wefindthatinthequalitativelongitudinalpositionthatwefirst
placedTarim on the basis of paleontologicalandgeological arguments (i.e., slightlyeast of Kazakhstan),
theTLIPislocated12.3±3.6°fromtheedgeofPerm.Withintherelativelysmalldirectionaluncertainty
associated withthe paleomagneticdata, this suggests that TLIPcould haveformed within ~10° of Perm,
which is comparable to the distance observed between some deeply sourced, modern‐day hot spots and
theLLSVPs(e.g.,Louisville).Thus,inaccordancewithboththequantitativepaleomagneticpaleolatitudinal

berelatabletothePermanomaly,andwespecificallyestimatetheTLIP's~290Malocationtohavebeen
29.9°N,~55–60°E.
Ifcorrect,ourproposedlinkbetweentheTLIPandPermwouldimplythatthelatterwasalreadypresentto
thenortheastoftheAfricanLLSVPbyearlyPermiantime,whichhasimportantimplicationsforthedebate
concerning LLSVP fixity (Bono et al., 2019; Torsvik et al., 2014), and the mobility of Perm in particular
(Flamentetal.,2017;Torsvik&Domeier,2017).ThelongevityandstabilityofPermanditssurfaceconnec-
tionsarealsokeytoanunderstandingofPermianpaleogeographymoregenerally.Forexample,Torsvik
et al. (2014) have related the ~252 Ma Siberian Traps to Perm, whereas Wu et al. (2017) have restored
Siberia ~15° to the west at that time using the paleomagnetic Euler pole method, allowing the Siberian
TrapstobeattributedtoeithertheplumenowfeedingtheIcelandhotspotorPerm(consideringthepaleo-
magnetic uncertainties). As another example, Flament et al. (2017) interpreted the Perm anomaly to be
highly mobile and proposed the ~260 Ma Emeishan LIP of south China to be derived from it, whereas
TorsvikandDomeier(2017)alternativelyascribetheEmeishanLIPtothePacificLLSVP.Resolutionofthese
importantpaleogeographicaldebateswillrequirefurtherdetailedpaleomagneticworkpairedwithconsid-
erationsofdeepmantledynamicsandtheirsurfaceconnections.
5. Conclusions
OurpaleomagneticstudyofearlyPermianrocksfromtheKepingareainnorthwesternTarimhasresultedin
theisolationofaprefoldingmagnetizationfrom51sitesofbothbasaltsandsedimentaryrocks.Thismagne-
tizationisofexclusivelyreversedpolarity,consistentwithitsacquisitionduringthelateCarboniferousto
mid‐Permian Kiaman Reversed Polarity Superchron. The resulting paleomagnetic pole computed from
theseresultsissimilartobothpreviouslypublishedearlyPermianpaleomagneticdatafromTarim,aswell
asearlyPermianreferencepolesfromthethen‐proximalcratonsoftheEastEuropeanCratonandSiberia.
This new paleomagnetic pole constrains the TLIP to have formed at a paleolatitude of 29.9°N ± 3.6.
AlthoughourattempttoconstrainthelongitudeofTarimaccordingtothePGZmethodrevealedthatitis
notpossibletorestoreTarimdirectlyaboveaLLSVPmargin,weobservethattherelativelongitudinalposi-
tionimpliedbyqualitativegeological/paleontologicaldataplacestheTLIPatadistanceof12.3±3.6°from
theedgeofPerm.AlthoughthisdistanceislargerthanthatinferredformostreconstructedLIPsoverthelast
300Ma(Torsviketal.,2014),itiscomparabletothedistancebetweensomedeeplysourced,modernhot
spots and the LLSVPs. We therefore estimate Tarim's early Permian longitudinal position to have been
~55–60°EandconjecturethattheTLIPcouldhavebeenrelatedtoPerm.Ifcorrect,thisimpliesthatPerm
waspresenttothenortheastoftheAfricanLLSVPbytheearlyPermian.
